To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

we have extended a previous model to include domain shrinkage, and we have developed a numerical approach for estimating the drift and diffusion terms for situations in which an analytic solution is not readily available.

we have derived an advection-difussion partial differential equation on growing and shrinking domains and demonstrated that it is a good approximation of our stochastic model, even when the drift and diffusion terms are unknown.

we have developed a general framework to derive FPEs for stochastic models of domain growth/shrinkage, we have demonstrated that our approach is valid for a variety of domain growth/shrinking mechanisms, and that it provides an accurate approximation of the stochastic model for a variety of different initial particle distributions.
In summary, our research is concerned with
developing a general framework for incorporating domain growth (and shrinkage) into individual-based stochastic models of biological phenomena.
the development of individual-based stochastic models of tissue growth and shrinkages and the derivation of FPEs for these models.
developing stochastic models of domain growth and shrinkage, and deriving Fokker-Planck equations which describe the dynamics of the probability density on the domain.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the FPE can be a useful tool in the analysis of stochastic models of domain growth and shrinkage, and that it can be used as an analytical tool to derive coefficients in situations where they are not readily available.
the Fokker-Planck Equation is an extremely useful tool for modelling the evolution of the mean density of particles in a stochastic system.
we can incorporate a range of domain growth mechanisms (and domain shrinkage) into a simple individual-based model of a tracer particle population.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we have developed a simple stochastic model for domain growth which allows a variety of different growth mechanisms to be incorporated and we have shown how the mean tracer density can be approximated using the solution of an FPE.

we have demonstrated that it is possible to derive a FPE from a basic stochastic model of domain expansion or contraction, that we have extended this work to incorporate a variety of domain growth mechanisms, that we are able in some cases to derive the coefficients of the FPE analytically and that we are able, in all cases, to estimate the coefficients numerically.
it is now possible to incorporate domain growth into a stochastic model, derive the corresponding FPE and estimate the coefficients of the FPE using our numerical approach.
The main takeaway from our work is that
it demonstrates the potential for deriving FPEs in a variety of different settings, even in cases in which the domain growth or shrinkage mechanisms are not readily available in an analytical form.

we are able, using simple stochastic models, to derive FPEs for a range of domain growth and shrinkage mechanisms and to obtain accurate estimates for the coefficients of these equations when the drift and diffusion are unknown.
it demonstrates that a stochastic model can be used to derive an advection-difusion FPE on an evolving domain, even if the underlying growth mechanism is not known a priori.
